topic: Why you can't tickle yourself (cerebellar prediction)

fact_check.claim: The cerebellum predicts self-generated movements and attenuates the resulting somatosensory response; introducing a delay via a robotic 'tickle machine' can make self-tickling feel ticklish.
fact_check.source_hint: Blakemore, Wolpert & Frith, 'Why can't you tickle yourself?', Neuroreport (2000); standard neuroscience textbooks on corollary discharge / sensory attenuation. Verify wording before publishing.

hooks: Try tickling yourself. Nothing. Here's why.
Your brain cancels touch before you feel it.
Tickling isn't about your skin at all.
titles: Why You Physically Can't Tickle Yourself (It's Not Your Skin)
Your Brain Deletes This Sensation Before You Feel It
Scientists Made A Robot That Finally Let People Tickle Themselves

beats.vo: Try tickling yourself. Nothing. Here's why.
beats.visual: Extreme close-up of fingers hovering over a palm; hand twitches on frame 1; zero title card

beats.vo: Someone else makes you squirm. Your own fingers do nothing. Same skin.
beats.visual: Split screen: other person's hand vs own hand on the same palm

beats.vo: Your cerebellum predicts your own movements. It sends that prediction ahead, then cancels the sensation it already expected.
beats.visual: Simple animated brain diagram: arrow from cerebellum racing ahead to the skin

beats.vo: That's why a surprise touch lands, and a planned one disappears. Predictable equals invisible.
beats.visual: Two taps on the arm, one expected one from off-frame; zoom punch on the second

beats.vo: Then researchers added a delay. Suddenly, people could tickle themselves.
beats.visual: Lab-style robot arm with a foam tip; timer counting milliseconds; colour grade shifts warm

beats.vo: Break the prediction and the brake lifts. The brain only silences what it can forecast in time. A few hundred milliseconds of lag made the touch feel like someone else's.
beats.on_screen: 200 MS OF LAG = SOMEONE ELSE'S HAND
beats.visual: Split timeline animation: on-time touch greyed out, delayed touch lighting up

beats.vo: So tickling isn't about touch. It's about your brain failing to be surprised.
beats.visual: Back to the opening close-up of the palm; slow push-in
Final frame matches frame 1 exactly for a seamless loop

payoff: Tickling is a prediction error, not a kind of touch.
cta: Could you actually tickle yourself? Yes or no?

description:
Try tickling yourself. Nothing happens — and the reason has nothing to do with your skin.

Your cerebellum predicts your own movements and dampens the sensation before it arrives. When researchers added a short delay with a robot, self-tickling suddenly worked.

Could you actually tickle yourself? Yes or no?

Concept: sensory attenuation / corollary discharge (Blakemore, Wolpert & Frith). Educational summary, not medical advice.
